As someone who is aggressively pro AI, I've also noticed how awful everything is to read lately. I find I routinely start reading interesting posts and just .. stop part way, abandoning it. A site I read stories on has been flooded with AI generated content, all of it terrible, and it just makes me retreat to things created before 2023 as a way of filtering it all out.

> uncanny valley of proseAh good ol' serendipity. I strongly believe this too, and I think that's why older (less capable) models fared better: they hadn't fallen into the valley yet. Had the pleasure of working with Jason Garrett-Glaser (better known as DarkShikari) circa 2011 on a patch for x264 to better utilize more cores (slice-threaded lookahead). At the time he was working with Sony to optimize their PlayStation game streaming service, and this had the potential to lower encoding latency (critical to game streaming) even on same-core systems by spreading the frame over more cores to do more parallel work, and doing more intelligent scheduling and convergence after that tile-based work was reconverged into a frame. At the time we were using servers with 48 physical cores to do transcoding, a bit of a rarity in a single NUMA space back then and there were no instances to test this on so I flamegraph traced a few encodes at very high thread parallel counts and send back the instrumented profiles (from a custom compiled version) showing the core work being done and he used that to optimize the motion estimation code which worked on the first shot to perfectly level out cpu usage and increase encoding speed across ~24 cores (was previously topping out around 8 and running one core hot iirc). I got a look into how exotic and complex this project was, particularly in terms how low level and advanced things like motion estimation, quantizing and perceptual compression were... it was and still is sort of magic how many smart techniques are baked into something that we barely pay attention to. They were, even at that time, working on x265.His blog, Diary of an x264 developer, was a great read too for anyone wanting to get a vantage point on how crazy that codebase was.[1]https://github.com/mstorsjo/x264/blob/master/doc/threads.txt(edit: was Gaikai that was acquired by Sony in 2012 and is the basis for PlayStation Now)

It is time to make a standard neural network for video, which guesses the next frame and/or applies super-resolution like DLSS does, so the necessary information to transmit is reduced to the minimum necessary for DLSS to reproduce the image without loss.
Ten years later, 2026 magic: AV1https://engineering.fb.com/2026/06/22/video-engineering/adop...And soon AV2https://av2.aomedia.org/

articles.title: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014)
articles.summary: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014)

top_comments: One of the great things about the movie is how children are portrayed. When the sea plane pirates take a bunch of kids hostage at the beginning of the movie, you don’t see any parents panicking. The kids are relaxed. The pirates clearly understand the social contract where they can’t split up the kids from their friends.It’s such a different take from modern parenting and today’s anxiety filled culture.

An aside, my 8yo son used Porco Rosso as the subject of a school speech about a favourite film. I was surprised how few of the themes were lost on him, especially those of war, comradeship, and the other side of every coin. Not to mention those points that only a child discovering the world can savour, that I'd missed myself (or at least misplaced since I first saw the film at around his age in the 90s).
For my money, one of the most visually impressive Ghibli movies. Just stunning composition throughout.
